SM19L-B1.free_elimination: 52.5 and 67.5 are a mirror pair about the catch-up point (60 km, +/-7.5): the 'behind' and 'ahead' twins of the same equation. A guesser who spots the twin pair keeps it and takes the larger, since 'ahead' means farther from the dock, which strikes 52.5. 63 is the catch-up distance plus the printed 3, but 60 is not printed, so it is not a one-step echo. 107.5 is not ruled out by any range bound without the catch-up arithmetic. Plugging back (B-3 = 12(B/20+2)) needs a computation per option, not a glance.
SM19L-B1.note: Cold solve: s hours after 10:00, 20s = 12(s+2)+3, 8s = 27, s = 3.375, B at 67.5 km. Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake. Difficulty: the obvious setup (B's time s, A's time s+2) lands straight on the key. The 107.5 trap needs a student to measure from 8:00 and then also use B's speed, which a competent student does not do, so there is no decision point that procedure skips. Medium. Repair: the mirror twin is built into an ahead/behind item, so any 'behind' distractor brings the tell back. Drop 52.5 for an error that lands above 60 and is neither key +/- 3 nor the A-position twin (64.5 = key - 3 is a closure tell). I found no natural candidate that passes every class, so the cleaner fix is to change the ask, e.g. 'how many minutes after boat B leaves is it 3 km ahead' with distractors from the 8:00 base (322.5) and from catch-up+3/20 h (189). Re-run the audit on any new set.

SM19L-B2.free_elimination: 12 dies to a magnitude floor: total time stays 126 = 42*3 minutes and no track is longer than 7 minutes, so the playlist needs at least 126/7 = 18 tracks. Two further strikes need insight, not a glance, so they are not counted. (a) The 7-minute tracks fill more than half the 126 minutes, so there are at least 9 of them, the total is at most 42 - 4*9/3 = 30, and 34 dies. (b) Each 7-for-3 swap is 7 three-minute tracks out and 3 seven-minute tracks in, so the total is 42 - 4k, which is 2 mod 4, and 12 and 28 both die.
SM19L-B2.note: Cold solve: 7x + 3y = 126 and 7x - 3y = 42 give x = 12 and y = 14, total 26. Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake. Difficulty: the 'minutes, not tracks' reading is the only decision, and writing the two equations in minutes is the routine setup. 12 is a reading slip (answering the 7-minute count), not a procedure trap. Medium. Repair: replace 12 with a value of at least 18 that is 2 mod 4, so it survives the floor and the swap-parity insight. 22 qualifies (15 seven-minute + 7 three-minute, from reading 'accounts for 42 more minutes' as twice that gap, L - S = 84), but that mistake is weak. 18 (both minute totals divided by 7) sits exactly on the floor, so a guesser could strike it as the extreme. Recommend 22 with a better-motivated origin, or re-author.

SM19L-B3.free_elimination: 5866 dies on divisibility. Every printed quantity (4200, 340, and 1890/7 = 270) is a multiple of 10 and the elapsed time is a whole number of days, so the stock must be a multiple of 10, and 5866 is the only option that is not. The stronger congruence (the stock is 4200 + 70d, so a multiple of 70, which would also kill 7030) needs the net rate of 70, which is the item's own arithmetic, so it is not counted. 7030 also exceeds a 4-week upper bound (4200 + 4*490 = 6160), but that needs the weekly net, so it is not counted either.
SM19L-B3.note: Cold solve: 1890/7 = 270 per day, net +70 per day, 25 days, 4200 + 1750 = 5950. Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake. Difficulty: converting the units to days is routine. The '3.4 weeks' and '34 days' traps catch careless students, not competent ones. Medium, bordering on easy. Repair: replace 5866 with a multiple of 70 from a natural error. 5670 = 4200 + 70*21 (stock after the 3 weeks, the 4 days dropped) passes the divisibility and range classes. Check its closures: 5670, 5950 and 6580 do not form an arithmetic progression (gaps 280 and 630), and 5950 is not the mean of any two of {5670, 6580, 7030}.

SM19L-B4.free_elimination: Adjacency tell: 16 and 17 are the only adjacent pair in an item explicitly about strict versus non-strict ('less than 40'). A guesser keeps the off-by-one pair, which strikes 22 and 25, and the strict 'less than' then points to the smaller member, 16. There is also a bound check: 40/1.25 = 32 and 12.5/1.25 = 10 are one-step divisions of printed numbers. They cap the count at 22 (n = 10..31) even with a weightless frame, and a 7.5 kg frame must lower that, so 22 and 25 both die.
SM19L-B4.note: Cold solve: 7.5 + 1.25n < 40 gives n < 26, so n <= 25; 1.25n >= 12.5 gives n >= 10; values 10..25 make 16. Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake. Difficulty: the strict-inequality fencepost is the only decision, and it is a drilled one. Medium. Repair: make the set four consecutive integers so the pair tell disappears and the bound strike reaches nothing, e.g. {14, 15, 16, 17}. 15 = 'at least 12.5' read as strict (n >= 11, values 11..25); 14 = that same strict lower end plus a dropped +1 in the count (25 - 11); 17 = 'less than' read as 'at most'. All four sit under the 22 ceiling. A four-run has no middle-of-three tell, and the key is not an endpoint.

SM19L-B5.free_elimination: Monotonicity: a + b = N(1), the 2019 value. The model rises (340 in 2021 to 610 in 2027), so N(1) < 340, and 370 and 385 die with no arithmetic. Seeing that a + b is the model's value at t = 1 is a single glance at the expression, and it is exactly the concept the item claims to test. 280 and 250 then need the slope.
SM19L-B5.note: Cold solve: t = 3 and t = 9 give a + 3b = 340 and a + 9b = 610, so b = 45, a = 205, and a + b = 250. Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake. Difficulty: the 't counts from 2018' decision is real, but writing the two equations from the stated t is routine, so a competent student reaches the key. Medium. Repair: put every distractor below 340 so monotonicity strikes nothing, e.g. {160, 250, 280, 295}. 295 = 2021 miscounted as t = 2 (and 2027 as t = 8), so b = 45 and a = 250. 160 = a - b, a sign slip in the last step. 280 is kept. Closure check: the gaps from 250 are 90, 30 and 45, there is no arithmetic progression, and 250 is not the mean of any two others (220, 227.5 and 287.5 are the pair means). Avoid 205, the bare a, because 205, 250 and 295 form an arithmetic progression with the key in the middle.

SM19L-B6.free_elimination: 470 = 40/0.085 and 666 = 40/0.06 are both one-step quotients of printed numbers, the budget over a printed rate with the printed fee ignored, so both are strikeable as echoes. 666 also dies by a glance-level magnitude check: 666 pages at the lowest rate already cost about $40 (39.96) before the $12 fee. 470 also dies by a quick plug-in: it is at least 400, so 0.06*470 = 28.2, and 28.2 + 12 > 40. With those two gone, 329 and 466 are both feasible orders, and 'greatest' picks 466.
SM19L-B6.note: Cold solve: $28 left after the fee. At 0.085, p <= 329.4; at 0.06, p <= 466.7, and 466 >= 400, so the 0.06 tier applies. Max is 466 (cost $39.96). Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake. Difficulty: the tier decision is a genuine trap. A student who prices at the first-listed, under-400 rate gets 329, finds 329 < 400 consistent, and stops, so hard as authored. That only holds because 329 is the sole feasible distractor, and the two echo distractors weaken it. Blueprint: piecewise cost read as a linear inequality per tier, which is acceptable but borderline. Repair: replace 666 with 266 = (40 - 24)/0.06, the fee counted twice. It is not a one-step echo and is feasible but smaller, so 'greatest' still needs the tier decision. For 470 I found no natural error that lands above 466, is infeasible, and is not a printed one-step quotient. 467 (rounding 466.67 up) makes an adjacent pair with the key as the lower member, which matches 'at most' and is a tell. 400 is a printed echo. And with only feasible smaller distractors the key becomes the largest option on a 'greatest' question. Recommend re-authoring the numbers so one fee-respecting error lands above the key, e.g. a fee that is mistakenly applied per 100 pages, then re-audit.

SM19L-B7.free_elimination: 2832 dies to a glance-level magnitude bound. Monday's 1140 includes 3 hours of both machines running, so 3(a + b) < 1140 and 6(a + b) < 2280. 1368 also dies to an averaging bound: it is 6 times Monday's average hourly output (1140/5 = 228), and that average mixes in 2 hours of machine A alone, so it must be strictly below a + b. That makes 1368 too small, by an inequality alone with no system solve. 1710 = 1.5*1140 is a one-step multiple of a printed number, but no condition rules it out cheaply.
SM19L-B7.note: Cold solve: 5a + 3b = 1140 and 3a + 5b = 1220; adding gives 8(a + b) = 2360, a + b = 295, and 6 hours make 1770 (a = 127.5, b = 167.5, positive). Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake. Difficulty: the add-the-equations shortcut is elegant, but the routine path (solve the system in Desmos, then compute 6(a + b)) also reaches the key, so there is no decision point that procedure bypasses. Medium. Repair: replace 2832 with a value inside the bounds (1368 to 2280) from a stated error, e.g. 1530 = 12*127.5 (machine A's rate used for both). Do not also add 2010 = 12*167.5, because 1530 and 2010 average to the key (closure). Preferably also replace 1368, which the averaging insight kills. Note that 1830 (Tuesday only, 1.5*1220) would make 1710, 1770, 1830 an arithmetic progression with the key in the middle, so avoid it.

SM19L-B8.free_elimination: none. All four options are integers; there is no parity or divisibility condition, no range bound beyond n > 1, and no option is a one-step combination of printed numbers. 31 = (132 - 70)/2 is two steps, and 30 and 14 need the full setup. Plugging back needs a multiplication and a division per option. There is a soft heuristic: a 2-year drop after removing the oldest member and adding six young ones implies a large club, which favours the largest option, but it is an estimate (about 108/n = 2), not a strike. The 30/31 adjacent pair does not contain the key, so the adjacency tell points away from it.
SM19L-B8.note: Cold solve: 34n - 70 + 6(22) = 32(n - 1 + 6), so 34n + 62 = 32n + 160, 2n = 98, n = 49. Check: 1666 + 62 = 1728, and 1728/54 = 32. Every distractor is reachable by its stated mistake, and 30 and 14 are real bookkeeping traps. Difficulty: there is a bookkeeping decision (the founder's 70 leaves both the total and the count), but writing total = mean * count before and after is the routine procedure and it reaches the key. Borderline hard, graded medium. Blueprint: mean context, solved as a linear equation in one variable; acceptable. No repair needed for elimination. To push it to hard, make one trap survive the routine setup, e.g. state the new members' combined age instead of their mean, or make the founder's age the unknown.
